<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but CON's rebuttal work was more precise and did more damage to live claims. CON caught PRO's fragmentation argument in a genuine logical error (a single streamer can consolidate a whole package regardless of whether some games stay free, so fragmentation is orthogonal to the free/paywall question), and PRO's reply in A4.5 simply reasserted the point rather than answering the counterexample. CON also exposed a real inconsistency in PRO's "accidental discovery" mechanism (B4.5: why can't a guest discover the sport watching a subscription final at a friend's house, just as at a free broadcast?), and PRO's closing never directly answered this, instead pivoting to a new "irreversibility" tie-breaker framing. CON's pressure question on defining "meaningful share" and its funding threshold (B3.1) was never squarely answered by PRO (A4.1 stayed vague, and B4.7 correctly called this out), leaving a live, unresolved burden on PRO's own proposal. PRO's case remained rhetorically vivid (commons, pipeline, shopfront window) and its closing precautionary-asymmetry argument was a smart strategic move, but it arrived late and CON's closing response (development losses are equally hard to recover, rights deals can be renegotiated) blunted its force. On balance CON's tighter, more responsive rebuttals and successful exposure of unresolved gaps in PRO's affirmative case give it a modest, competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's B4.5 puncturing of PRO's "accidental discovery" distinction (why can a guest discover a sport at a subscription-final barbecue but not through household viewing of an ordinary game?) was the most damaging single exchange, since PRO never directly rehabilitated the distinction afterward.</best_rebuttal>
